scenes.heading: Data Mesh
scenes.narration: Data Mesh is an organizational and architectural approach that decentralizes data ownership to the domains that know the data best, treating data as a product.

scenes.heading: The four principles
bullets: Data as a product with clear contracts
scenes.narration: The first principle is domain ownership: the teams closest to the data own and serve it analytically, rather than a central team. The second is treating data as a product, with owners accountable for its quality, documentation, and service-level guarantees. The third is a self-serve platform that gives domains the tooling to publish and consume data without central bottlenecks. The fourth is federated computational governance, where global rules like security and interoperability are automated and enforced across all domains.

scenes.heading: Data Mesh vs centralized platform
scenes.narration: In a Data Mesh each domain owns and serves its data as a product, which scales well across a large organization because no single team is a chokepoint, but it demands a mature self-serve platform and strong federated governance to avoid chaos. A centralized platform has one team owning the warehouse, which is simple and coherent in a smaller organization, but that team becomes a bottleneck and loses domain context as the company grows. Mesh is a response to scaling pain, not a default for every team.

scenes.heading: How a data product is served
steps: Publishes a data product with contract
scenes.narration: A domain team owns its source systems and the pipelines that shape its data. It publishes a data product with a documented interface, schema contract, and quality guarantees. That product is registered in the shared catalog so it is discoverable. Federated governance policies for security, privacy, and interoperability are applied automatically by the platform. Other domains then discover the product in the catalog and consume it through its stable contract, without needing to know its internals.

scenes.heading: What makes a good data product
bullets: Discoverable and addressable in the catalog
scenes.narration: For a mesh to work, each data product must meet a bar sometimes summarized as being discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, self-describing, interoperable, and secure. Being discoverable and addressable means others can find and reference it in the catalog. Being trustworthy means it publishes and honors quality and freshness service-level objectives. Being self-describing means its schema and documentation stand on their own. And being interoperable means it follows common standards so products from different domains can be joined together easily.

scenes.heading: Common failure modes
bullets: Mesh adopted without a real platform
Too small an org to justify the overhead
scenes.narration: Data Mesh fails in predictable ways. Adopting the philosophy without first building the self-serve platform leaves domains unable to actually ship products. Domains without data engineering skills produce low-quality products or none at all. Governance that is too loose leads to inconsistent, unjoinable data and a compliance mess. And in a small organization the coordination overhead simply is not worth it, since a central team would serve everyone perfectly well. Mesh is a scaling remedy, not a starting point.

scenes.text: Data Mesh trades central control for domain autonomy; adopt it when scale hurts, and only with a strong platform and governance.
scenes.narration: Data Mesh trades central control for domain autonomy and product thinking, which pays off when a central team has become a scaling bottleneck, but only succeeds when backed by a strong self-serve platform and automated federated governance.
